title: SPATIAL ORIENTATION AND THE ANGULARITY OF URBAN ROUTES A Field Study
research_question: To examine the influence of urban route angularity on the spatial orientation (pointing accuracy and speed) of pedestrians, specifically contrasting effects on local features versus global reference frames (cardinal directions).

participants.description: 18 female and 42 male, most between 19 and 26 years of age (range 17-50). Fifty were university staff, students, or faculty. All subjects were residents of Tempe, Arizona.
participants.recruitment: Pedestrians were stopped on the sidewalk at one of three testing locations and asked to participate in a study on city layout knowledge.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Three urban street locations in a homogeneous area of off-campus university housing in Tempe, Arizona. Locations were: 1) Lemon Street (orthogonal, east-west, coincident with local grid), 2) Terrace Road (oblique 1, northwest-southeast diagonal, directly connected to major grid streets), and 3) Orange Street (oblique 2, northeast-southwest diagonal, secondarily connected via Terrace). All locations were within 140m of each other, and no distant landmark cues were visible.

measures.instrument: Absolute pointing error (degrees) to five nonvisible targets (Gammage Auditorium, corner of Rural and University, parallel to Apache Boulevard, South, Northeast) using a rotatable wire pointer.
Response time (seconds) to point to nonvisible targets, measured manually with a stopwatch.
7-point Likert scale (1=not at all familiar, 7=perfectly familiar) for street layout within a half mile of the testing location.
Self-reported estimate of how many times walked by the testing location in an average week.
Self-reported number of months lived in the Tempe area.

mechanisms: Memory distortion or imprecision associated with oblique routes.

Difficulty in coordinating body-centered orthogonal axes with environmental orthogonal axes (local features or global frames) when navigating oblique routes, leading to less accurate memory representations and spatial updating.
Increased cognitive load and response time due to the need to access spatial knowledge via anchoring routes or landmarks when navigating less connected oblique routes.
moderators: Target type (local feature vs. cardinal direction)
implementation_implications: Urban design with orthogonal street patterns may facilitate spatial orientation and reduce memory distortion for routes and cardinal directions.
The presence of highly visible and salient landmark features could help counteract disorientation caused by oblique routes.

tables.description: Intercorrelations of Response Time, Pointing Error, and Familiarity Questions

limitations: Nonrandom assignment of subjects to testing locations.
Confounding of multiple aspects of route angularity (e.g., deviation from local grid, deviation from cardinal directions, number of oblique turns) within the existing urban environment.

paper_metadata.title: Spatial Orientation and the Angularity of Urban Routes
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Spatial Orientation and the Angularity of Urban Routes
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: The influence of route angularity on the spatial orientation of pedestrians navigating in an urban field setting was examined. Sixty pedestrians were stopped at one of three locations in the same neighborhood, one on a street orthogonal to the local grid pattern and two on streets oblique to the local grid pattern. They were asked to point to several nonvisible targets, both local features and cardinal directions. Pointing error on four of the five targets was greater on both oblique streets than on the orthogonal street, especially for the cardinal directions; response time was greater only on the second oblique street, a secondary street that is connected to the local grid system via the first oblique street. Length of residency was related to both accuracy and response speed. Results demonstrate that environmental orientation depends in part on the angularity of route structure, the disorienting effect of oblique routes being due to memory distortion or imprecision associated with oblique routes.
